review_theme: Honey flow depends on controlled geometry and head
individual_teacher_note: More viscous honey tends to drain more slowly than water under otherwise comparable conditions, but the word 'mainly' implicitly assumes comparable cup tilt, fill level, temperature and driving pressure; viscosity is not a stand-alone universal flow-rate predictor.
Most ordinary liquids, including honey, become less viscous when warmed; composition or temperature-dependent structural changes can affect details but source answer A remains appropriate.

At a comparable relative air speed, holding a hand edge-on usually lowers frontal area and drag; real drag also depends on shape and drag coefficient. This is a conceptual example, not an instruction to put hands outside moving vehicles.
With comparable orientation and ambient air conditions, increasing relative speed typically increases air resistance; the car speed itself is a proxy only if air is approximately still.
Mass and speed held fixed do not fix drag: orientation can change effective projected area and drag coefficient for a body in flow.

review_theme: V-formation figure and intended drag benefit
individual_teacher_note: The prepared teacher source states geese in V-formation can reduce aerodynamic effort; the original GitHub bank references unit6-figure63. Claim of what the original printed NBF Figure 6.3 exactly shows/captions requires printed image verification. Aerodynamic saving depends on relative positions/upwash, not merely group shape.
Swimmers and skydivers change effective area and shape to change drag; unlike the low-Reynolds sphere, these require more general drag models.
A raindrop can reach constant downward speed when upward drag balances its effective downward weight. The source explicitly uses a simplified model treating buoyancy as negligible.
At release from rest in STILL air, relative velocity initially vanishes, so motion-dependent drag is approximately zero; ambient wind would change the initial relative speed.
Under the stated textbook approximation neglecting buoyancy, downward mg equals upward drag; the drop still falls at constant nonzero terminal speed.

review_theme: Upward net force slows a still-descending parachutist
individual_teacher_note: Immediately after deployment, upward drag may temporarily exceed downward weight, giving upward acceleration while the parachutist is STILL moving downward; source answer C does not imply upward instantaneous motion. Real parachute drag cannot be computed via Stokes small-sphere law.
v_t=2ρ_sgr²/(9η) is the simplified buoyancy-neglecting model, with sphere density and viscosity fixed; actual v_t depends on ρ_s−ρ_f and model validity.
Doubling radius predicts v_t increased by factor 4 only if physical parameters and the slow-flow Stokes regime are still applicable. This is not a universal falling-body speed scaling.
Tripling η predicts one-third model terminal speed with droplet density, radius, g and all other relevant fluid conditions held fixed. No blanket statement for all flows.

The source's simplified v_t∝ρ_s scaling gives D (double) only when the buoyant-density subtraction is neglected. With buoyancy included, v_t∝(ρ_s−ρ_f) and doubling ρ_s does NOT generally double v_t. Preserve source D for the explicitly simplified model only.
If diameter doubles, radius doubles, so r² becomes (2r)²=4r². This is a geometry/proportionality task rather than direct viscous-force explanation.
For equal-density uniform spheres m=ρ_s(4/3)πr³; doubling radius means mass multiplied by 8. A fundamental sphere geometry relation, item-level official SLO scope still pending.

review_theme: Sphere mass formula and density label
individual_teacher_note: For uniform sphere, m=ρ_s(4/3)πr³ uses the sphere's MATERIAL density, not surrounding fluid density; source A is correct.
For fixed relative speed and η within Stokes creeping-flow regime, F_d=6πηrv makes doubling r double drag, even though terminal speed scales with r² in a distinct model.

review_theme: Net force gives acceleration, not immediate travel direction
individual_teacher_note: Weight larger than upward drag gives a downward resultant and thus downward acceleration IF other vertical forces/buoyancy are negligible. It does not alone prove an object was already moving downward or is instantly at constant speed.
